target: La plaza está llena de gente.
english: The square is full of people.
tip: "Estar" for temporary states. The square is full now, but it won't always be.

target: Lo arregló mi padre en cinco minutos.
english: My father fixed it in five minutes.
tip: Subject after the verb! "Lo arregló mi padre" fronts the fix and saves the fixer for last – Spanish pushes the news to the end. English word order isn't law here.

target: Salimos para el aeropuerto a las cinco.
english: We left for the airport at five.
tip: "Para" indicates destination: we left heading toward the airport.

target: Nada es imposible cuando trabajamos todos juntos.
english: Nothing is impossible when we all work together.
tip: "Nada es imposible" needs no extra no – a negative word before the verb stands alone. After the verb, the double negative becomes mandatory: no hay nada.

target: Tardé media hora en llegar al centro.
english: It took me half an hour to get downtown.
tip: English blames "it" (it took me); Spanish makes YOU the subject: "tardé" = I took-time. Tardar en + infinitive – the person doing it is the subject.

target: Busqué mi equipaje por toda la cinta.
english: I looked for my luggage all along the conveyor belt.
tip: "Buscar" already contains the "for": busqué mi equipaje = I looked FOR my luggage. The por here means all over (por toda la cinta) – never use por to mean "for" after buscar.

target: Cada estudiante debe traer su propio material de clase.
english: Each student must bring their own class materials.
tip: "Su" can mean his, her, their, or your (usted). Context decides – here "su propio" pins it to each student. Spanish leaves this ambiguous where English can't.

target: Hay juguetes en el suelo.
english: There are toys on the floor.
tip: Hay = there is/there are (invariable, same for singular and plural).

target: No hablo español muy bien.
english: I don't speak Spanish very well.
tip: Languages go lowercase: "español", never Español. Spanish capitalizes much less than English – languages, nationalities, days, and months are all lowercase.

target: No como carne, soy vegetariano.
english: I don't eat meat, I'm vegetarian.
tip: No "a" needed: "soy vegetariano", not un vegetariano. With ser + identity (jobs, diets, religions), Spanish drops the article – you ARE the category itself.

target: Paso tres días en Barcelona.
english: I spend three days in Barcelona.
tip: Two verbs for spend: "paso tres días" – pasar for time, gastar for money. Swap them and gasté tres días suggests the days were burned through, wasted.

target: Hay ropa en la lavadora.
english: There are clothes in the washing machine.
tip: Clothes are plural in English, but "ropa" is singular: hay ropa, la ropa está. One shirt or a whole laundry load – still just ropa.

target: Los lunes son los días más difíciles.
english: Mondays are the hardest days.
tip: Days carry their own article: "los lunes" = Mondays. And no "on" – el lunes is this Monday, los lunes every Monday. Saying en lunes is the English-speaker tell.

target: Ayer no había nadie en la oficina.
english: Yesterday there was nobody in the office.
tip: Why había, not hubo? Había paints the scene – the office sat empty all day. Hubo would report a one-off event, which an ongoing state of emptiness isn't.

target: Perdón, ¿por dónde se va al centro?
english: Excuse me, how do you get to the center?
tip: "¿Por dónde se va?" is literally "by where does one go?" – se makes it impersonal, no "you" required. Spanish asks about the route, not the person walking it.

target: Hoy desayuné solo un yogur con fruta.
english: Today I only had a yogurt with fruit for breakfast.
tip: Breakfast is a verb: "desayuné" = I breakfasted. No "have" needed – and it scales: almorzar (lunch), cenar (dinner). Each meal has its own verb.

target: Mi abuelo fumaba mucho pero lo dejó.
english: My grandfather used to smoke a lot but he quit.
tip: How does "lo dejó" (he left it) mean he quit? Dejar = leave behind – Spanish quits things by walking away from them. Fumaba mucho, pero lo dejó.

target: Ven aquí, necesito hablar contigo sobre algo importante.
english: Come here, I need to talk to you about something important.
tip: Con fuses with just three pronouns: conmigo, contigo, consigo – never 'con ti'. That -go tail is a Latin fossil: 'with' got stuck on both ends of the word.

target: No existe nadie que pueda resolver esto solo.
english: There's nobody who can solve this alone.
tip: English drops one negative; Spanish stacks them. No existe nadie is the required double – 'existe nadie' on its own would just sound broken, not emphatic.

target: Perfecto, entonces quedamos a las ocho en punto.
english: Perfect, then we'll meet at eight o'clock sharp.
tip: "Quedamos" – quedar normally means to remain, but between people it means we're meeting up. It's THE plan-making verb in Spain: quedamos a las ocho seals the deal.

target: Me contó que de pequeño quería ser astronauta.
english: He told me that as a child he wanted to be an astronaut.
tip: Not "un astronauta"! Spanish drops the article for professions after ser: "quería ser astronauta" – the a/an English demands just isn't there.

target: El plan parecía bueno; ahora bien, necesitamos más datos.
english: The plan seemed good; however, we need more data.
tip: "Ahora bien" = now then / however. Introduces a reservation or counterpoint to what was just said.

target: Los niños de hoy saben más de tecnología que nosotros.
english: Kids today know more about technology than we do.
tip: "Saben de" = know about facts and fields: saben más de tecnología. For knowing people or places, Spanish switches verbs to conocer – knowledge vs acquaintance.

target: Intento no usar el celular durante la comida, pero no siempre lo consigo.
english: I try not to use my phone during meals, but I don't always manage to.
tip: That tiny lo in lo consigo stands for the whole idea 'not using my phone during meals'. One pronoun can swallow an entire clause in Spanish.

target: Ella está embarazada.
english: She's pregnant.
tip: Embarazada means pregnant – never embarrassed. It's the classic false friend: if you're embarrassed, say tengo vergüenza or estoy avergonzada.

target: Ella es soltera.
english: She's single.
tip: Ser for civil status: "Es casada." Marital status uses ser – it defines identity, not a passing state.

target: Ella lleva gafas.
english: She wears glasses.
tip: Wear or carry? Spanish doesn't care – llevar does both. 'Lleva gafas' = she wears glasses, literally 'she carries glasses.'

target: Pregúntale al recepcionista.
english: Ask the receptionist.
tip: Why say 'him' twice? 'Pregúntale al recepcionista' = 'ask-HIM to-the receptionist.' Spanish doubles the person with le even when they're named.

target: Hace mucho viento.
english: It's very windy.
tip: Windy isn't something it IS – it's something it MAKES. Weather uses hacer: 'Hace mucho viento' = it makes much wind.

target: Soy diseñador gráfico.
english: I'm a graphic designer.
tip: No 'a' before jobs! English says 'I'm A designer'; Spanish drops the article with ser + profession: 'Soy diseñador gráfico.'
